title: 一次难忘的旅行
text:
The Dormouse’s Unforgettable Moonlit Journey
(A gentle bedtime tale for little listeners)

Deep in Twilight Thicket, where old oak trees wore moss like fuzzy green socks, lived a tiny dormouse named Dormie.
His fur was the color of toasted oat crumbs. His tail was fluffier than dandelion down. And his very favorite thing in the whole wide world was sparkly, sweet snacks.

One soft September evening, Grandma Dormouse tucked a dandelion-fluff scarf around his neck.
“Tonight is the harvest moon,” she whispered. “Follow the gurgle of the silver stream, and you will find Moonberry Hollow. The moonberries there glow like little star candies. They ripen only one night a year.”

Dormie grabbed his tiny acorn basket, wiggled his whiskers, and pattered off before the first star had even blinked open.

He’d hopped over only three toadstools when he heard a tiny, wobbly sniffle.
Stuck to a clover leaf sat Flick, a baby firefly. His thin gossamer wings were gummed with dewdrop honey, and he could not glow bright enough to find his way to the hollow’s firefly dance.
“Oh dear,” said Dormie. He leaned in very gently, and dabbed Flick’s wings dry with the soft tip of his fluffy tail.

Flick flickered once, twice, then glowed warm gold—like a tiny floating candle.
“Thank you!” he buzzed. “I will light every step for you, I promise.”

They pattered and glided on, until the silver stream curled across their path. The water gurgled like a lullaby, but Dormie’s tiny paws could not swim across.
Just then, a round cream-colored mushroom drifted toward the bank. Perched on its cap was Grandma Slowbell, a snail with polka dots on her shell, poling slowly with a thin blade of grass.
“Room for two small ones,” she rumbled, slow and sweet as warm honey tea. “This mushroom ferry is heading for the hollow too.”

Dormie climbed on very carefully. Flick perched softly on his ear. The mushroom rocked gentle as a cradle as it drifted. Reeds whispered quiet secrets along the bank, and Dormie yawned so wide his little ears wiggled.
“Almost there,” Flick hummed, tickling his ear lightly.

When they rounded the bend, Moonberry Hollow bloomed right in front of them.
Hundreds of tiny velvety blue berries glowed all over low, soft bushes, like starlight spilled on grass. The air smelled like honey and lavender, and crickets chirped a slow waltz in the clover.

But by the very first bush, a tiny spiky ball was huffing and puffing. It was Bramble, the baby hedgehog. His legs were too short to reach the plumpest berries, and his prickles kept tangling in the leaves.
“Let’s help!” said Dormie.
He scrambled up the bush (he was very good at climbing oak roots, after all). Flick held his warm glow right over the juiciest fruit. Grandma Slowbell passed up a smooth lily pad to pile the berries on.

Soon Bramble had a little berry pile all his own. He crunched one, and his button eyes went wide.
“It tastes like stardust hot cocoa!” he squeaked.

They all sat on a flat sun-warmed stone, passing berries around. Flick ate one the size of a pinhead and glowed bright pink for ten whole minutes. Grandma Slowbell nibbled hers so slowly it lasted the whole ferry ride home. Dormie saved three of the plumpest, glowiest berries in his acorn basket: one for Grandma Dormouse, one for Flick to take to the dance, and one to tuck under his pillow.

When Dormie trundled back to his mossy oak burrow, his paws were tired, his scarf was askew, and his heart felt as full and warm as a baked apple.
“Was the moonberry the best treat you ever had?” Grandma asked.

Dormie yawned, snuggling deep into his thistledown blanket. He thought of sticky firefly wings, the rocking mushroom ferry, and Bramble’s giggle when Flick glowed pink.
“The berries were lovely,” he mumbled, his eyelids drooping heavy. “But the best part… was the friends I found along the way. That is the part I will never forget.”

He took one tiny, sweet bite of his pillow berry. Its soft golden glow wrapped around him like a hug. Outside, the harvest moon beamed through oak leaves, crickets hummed slow and soft, and Dormie drifted off to the sweetest, sparkliest dreams.

✨ The End ✨

---
 Little reading tip for grown-ups:
Read in a slow, soft voice—pause to yawn when Dormie does, and whisper the glow/rocking parts. The calm, conflict-free rhythm is made to lull little ones to sleep.

title: 团队合作
text:
The Fern Line Path
(Word count: 498)
The intercollegiate wilderness orienteering race started as a half-joke for the four misfits of Pine Creek University’s outdoor club. Lila, the botany major who got lost walking to the campus dining hall three times her first semester, could identify every native plant within 50 paces but could not read a compass to save her life. Javi, the former cross-country runner sidelined by a knee injury, could tie 17 kinds of rescue knots but could barely jog a mile without limping. Mia, the studio art student with 800-degree myopia, could spot a half-centimeter paint scratch on a canvas across a room but could not make out standard trail markers 10 meters away in fog. Tao, the impulsive computer science major, could calculate elevation gains and optimal routes in his head in 10 seconds but regularly missed obvious turns by rushing ahead.
An hour into the 12-mile race, a sudden summer thunderstorm hit, washing away nearly all the bright orange official trail markers. Teams scattered: some yelled over the rain arguing about directions, others turned back to wait out the weather. Tao initially insisted on cutting straight up a steep shale slope to shave 20 minutes off the route, until Javi warned the slippery rock would send them sliding into the gully below. Then Lila, huddled under a pine bough, spoke up: “Interrupted ferns only grow along well-drained ridge lines—they never root in muddy, flood-prone ravines. If we follow the fern bands, we’ll stay on high, solid ground.”
The group fell into sync without a formal plan. Tao pulled out his crumpled topographic map, cross-referencing the fern-lined ridge Lila identified to map the fastest route that avoided cliff drop-offs. Javi, his knee braced, moved at the center of the line, twisting wild grapevines into temporary handholds on slick rock patches and retying everyone’s boot laces into the non-slip knots he learned in wilderness first aid. Mia, squinting through rain-spotted glasses, took the lead, spotting faint, mud-caked reflective tacks nailed to tree trunks by rangers years prior—tiny markers every other rushing team had missed in the downpour.
They crossed the finish line 12 minutes ahead of the closest team, soaked to the bone and streaked with pine sap and mud. When the race organizer asked which of them was the “star navigator,” they all laughed. None of them would have finished the route alone: the directionally challenged botanist, the injured runner, the nearsighted artist, the impulsive coder. But together, they had blazed a path no single person could have found. They used the $500 race prize to buy picture books and rain boots for the elementary school tucked at the base of the trail.

title: 小王子
text:
*The Little Prince*: Seeing the World Through the Heart
I first pulled Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s *The Little Prince* from a children’s bookshelf as a child, drawn to its soft, whimsical illustrations (drawn by the author himself) and the strange golden-haired boy visiting from a tiny asteroid. Back then, I read it as a sweet, slightly sad adventure story. When I reread it years later as a young adult navigating job applications, rental costs and all the unspoken rules of the “grown-up world”, I cried within the first twenty pages. This slim 1943 French novella is never just a fairy tale for children. It is a quiet, wise mirror held up to adults, reminding us of all the precious things we accidentally leave behind as we grow up.

The story follows the little prince, who lives alone on Asteroid B-612: a rock barely larger than a house, home to three volcanoes (one extinct, which he still cleans regularly) and a vain, delicate rose he loves deeply. Confused and hurt by the rose’s petty pride, he leaves his planet to travel the universe, and meets a string of absurd grown-ups on neighboring asteroids: a king who rules over no one but insists on his empty authority; a conceited man who only hears praise; a drunkard who drinks to forget the shame of drinking; and most memorably, a businessman who busily counts stars, convinced he “owns” them simply because he writes their numbers on paper.
These characters feel silly at first glance, but they perfectly mirror the values our adult world celebrates: chasing power, status, wealth and empty recognition without ever stopping to ask why. As the book sharply observes, grown-ups love numbers. They never ask, “What does his voice sound like? What games does he love best? Does he collect butterflies?” Instead, they ask, “How old is he? How much does he earn? How big is his house?” Too often, we reduce the whole world to measurable, usable facts, and miss the living, warm truth underneath.

It is the fox the prince meets in the Sahara Desert that gives the story its beating, timeless heart. When the fox asks the prince to “tame” him, he explains a simple yet profound truth: to tame someone means to build a unique bond, to make that person different from all the thousands of strangers in the world. “You become responsible forever for what you have tamed,” the fox says. “You are responsible for your rose.”
This lesson clicks for the prince when he stumbles on a garden full of five thousand roses identical to his own. For a moment he feels cheated and ordinary, convinced his rose lied about being one of a kind. But he soon realizes she is still irreplaceable: he has watered her, shielded her from cold wind with a screen, listened to her grumbles and her brags, and sat with her in silence. She is not special because she is rare by birth. She is special because he has given his time and care to her. That is the story’s most famous, enduring truth: *“It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.”* Love, loyalty, tenderness and belonging cannot be counted, bought or owned. They can only be felt, nurtured, and honored.

The unnamed pilot, stranded in the desert with a broken plane, is the first grown-up the prince meets who still remembers this truth. Together they search for a hidden well, and their quiet friendship turns the endless dry sand into something magical. When the prince chooses to let the snake bite him, to return to his rose on his distant asteroid, he does not frame it as an ending. His body is too heavy to carry all the way home, he explains, but his love for the rose stays. For the pilot, and for readers, his absence never erases their bond: whenever you look up at the night sky, it will be as if all the stars are laughing, like five hundred million little bells. Loved ones may be far away, or leave us entirely, but the time we gave them stays with us forever.

Rereading this book in an era obsessed with follower counts, bank balances, job titles and “optimizing” every minute of life, its message feels more urgent than ever. We are all encouraged to be the businessman, counting what we can claim as ours, instead of the little prince, stopping to care for one fussy, imperfect flower. We swipe through hundreds of faces online without ever taming a single true friend, and chase bigger and better prizes without noticing the small, gentle bonds that already make life rich.

*The Little Prince* is often shelved in children’s sections, but it is written for every grown-up who has forgotten they were once a child too: someone who knew a cardboard box holding an imaginary sheep can be far more wonderful than any expensive toy, and a single rose matters more than all the stars in the sky, if you love her. It does not give grand life advice. It only asks us to slow down, tend to what we love, and take responsibility for the bonds we build. On hard, noisy days, I still look up at the stars. Somewhere, I know, a little prince is watering his rose—and the whole world feels softer for it.

（全文约1050词，适合高中/大学低年级英语读书报告；如果需要缩短篇幅，可以删减旅途中成人角色的举例或现实关联段落，也可以替换为个人亲身经历呼应“驯服与责任”的主题）

title: 会说话的大树
text:
Phased Implementation Checklist: The Community Talking Tree (Zero-Damage Interactive Public Nature Installation) Project Overview This actionable, metric-driven checklist guides deployment of a Talking Tree: a community-centered, edge-AI-powered interactive installation mounted on a mature native tree in public parks or nature education camps. The setup uses hidden, tree-safe hardware to let visitors hold natural voice conversations with the tree, which shares local ecological knowledge, preserves collective community oral history, and facilitates nature-based play for children. All work adheres to three non-negotiable core principles: 1. Zero harm to the host tree, surrounding plants, and local wildlife 2. Community co-creation, free non-commercial access for all visitors 3. Privacy-by-design and universal accessibility for disabled guests --- Phase 1: Foundation, Co-Design & Regulatory Approval Timeline: Months 0–3 (Pre-development) | Actionable Checklist Items | Completed? | |-----------------------------|------------| | Form core project team: 1 project lead, 1 ISA-certified arborist, 1 community engagement coordinator, 1 tech lead, 1 certified accessibility consultant | ☐ | | Recruit a 40-person demographically balanced co-design panel: 10 seniors (65+), 10 children (7–12), 10 working-age local residents, 5 people with visual/auditory/mobility disabilities, 3 local ecologists, 2 park authority staff | ☐ | | Host 3 two-hour co-design workshops to:
• Vote on priority features (e.g., nature Q&A, community memory bank, kids’ scavenger hunt prompts)
• Define the Tree’s persona (e.g., 80-year-old native oak with a warm, rustling voice that shares neighborhood memories)
• Document accessibility requirements (hearing aid compatibility, braille controls, child-height access points) | ☐ | | Select host tree per mandatory criteria:
• Native mature tree ≥20 years old, with arborist-confirmed good health (no trunk decay, stable canopy, no root rot)
• Sited in a secondary pedestrian flow zone (10–15m from main paths, with ≥20sqm of shaded gathering space, no overhead power line conflicts)
• Access to dappled sunlight for solar power, no active bird/nest sites in the immediate installation zone
• Prioritize trees with existing community cultural significance (e.g., well-loved local landmark) | ☐ | | Complete full arborist assessment, including a root zone map to mark areas where no digging is permitted | ☐ | | Secure all required approvals: park land use permit, tree protection work permit, installation noise variance, data privacy compliance sign-off (aligned with local rules: GDPR, CCPA, PIPL, etc.) | ☐ | | Lock in 3 years of funding via public art grants, community foundation awards, and in-kind park support (no commercial sponsorships requiring on-site advertising) | ☐ | Deliverables Signed project charter, arborist health report for the host tree, all valid permits, prioritized feature list and Tree persona guide, 3-year locked budget Responsible Parties Project lead, certified arborist, community coordinator, park authority, legal/compliance advisor Success Metrics - 100% sign-off from the co-design panel on project scope - Selected host tree passes arborist assessment with zero high-risk health issues - All permits secured 2 weeks before prototype development begins - Full funding secured for the first 2 years of operation Risk Mitigation - Pre-identify 3 alternate host trees in case the first choice fails health or permit review - Hold a 15% budget contingency for unplanned tree protection or compliance costs --- Phase 2: Tree-Safe Hardware Customization & AI Prototype Development Timeline: Months 4–8 (R&D and prototyping) | Actionable Checklist Items | Completed? | |-----------------------------|------------| | Design zero-damage mounting systems meeting arborist standards:
• No drilling, nailing, or penetration of bark, cambium, or roots at any point
• Use width-adjustable, food-grade EPDM rubber straps for all mounts, pre-set with 2cm of slack to accommodate annual tree growth
• Distribute hardware weight across ≥4 separate trunk contact points to avoid bark pressure damage
• Run all low-voltage cables through 5cm-deep trenches along natural root gaps, covered with native soil and leaf mulch (no root cutting permitted) | ☐ | | Source IP67 weather-sealed hardware:
• Directional parametric speakers mounted 2m high in the lower canopy, with sound limited to a 3m radius to eliminate noise spillover
• Far-field microphone array with wind/noise cancellation, tuned to pick up normal speaking voices from 3m away while filtering wind, bird calls, and distant traffic
• Flexible solar panels mounted on an unobtrusive dark green post 2m from the tree (no panels mounted directly on the tree to avoid weight stress), connected to a low-voltage battery stored in a bark-mimicking faux tree hollow at the tree base
• Edge computing unit stored in the faux hollow, enabling 100% of core dialogue processing to run locally (no cloud dependency for basic functions)
• Accessibility add-ons: hearing loop for hearing aid users, braille touch panel on a 0.8m-high accessible post next to the tree, QR code linking to sign language video guides for Deaf visitors | ☐ | | Train the edge AI dialogue model to match the approved Tree persona:
• Build 3 core content modules: 200+ local ecology facts, 25 initial community oral histories collected from seniors during co-design, 3 interactive nature play prompts for children
• Integrate two-layer content moderation: on-device keyword filtering to block inappropriate queries, plus a human review queue for all visitor-submitted stories before they are added to the Tree’s memory bank
• Tune voice output to blend a warm, neutral human tone with 15% background rustling leaf sound effects to avoid uncanny valley effects; cap response latency at 1 second for natural conversation flow | ☐ | | Run 2 rounds of lab user testing with 120 demographically matched testers to refine speech recognition, volume levels, response tone, and accessibility feature usability | ☐ | | Conduct independent noise testing to confirm audio levels do not exceed 55dB at 10m from the tree (aligned with residential daytime noise standards) | ☐ | | Secure written arborist sign-off for the full hardware installation plan, confirming zero risk of tree damage | ☐ | Deliverables Arborist-approved zero-damage installation plan, V1.0 edge AI dialogue system, full set of accessibility-compliant weather-sealed hardware, user testing report with 95% of critical issues resolved Responsible Parties Hardware engineering team, AI training team, arborist, accessibility consultant, content development team Success Metrics - Hardware plan receives formal arborist sign-off confirming no drilling, no root damage, and sufficient growth slack for mounts - Speech recognition accuracy ≥90% for common user queries in simulated windy outdoor conditions - Noise testing confirms ≤55dB at 10m from speakers - Tester satisfaction score ≥4.5/5 across all age and ability groups Risk Mitigation - Test hardware in extreme temperature/heavy rain conditions to avoid weather-related failure - Build a one-tap manual content override to immediately disable inappropriate responses if moderation filters fail --- Phase 3: Low-Impact On-Site Installation & Soft Launch Timeline: Months 9–10 (Installation and limited real-world testing) | Actionable Checklist Items | Completed? | |-----------------------------|------------| | Schedule all installation work during the host tree’s dormant season (late fall/early spring, per local climate) to avoid disrupting growth, nesting birds, or pollinator activity | ☐ | | Post temporary construction fencing around the work zone 3 days in advance, with clear signs explaining the project for park visitors | ☐ | | Require the certified arborist to be on-site for 100% of installation hours, with authority to halt work immediately if any tree health risk is identified | ☐ | | Complete installation per the approved plan:
• Lay cables in shallow root-gap trenches, cover with native soil and leaf mulch (no soil compaction in the root zone)
• Attach rubber mounting straps, confirm 2cm slack before mounting speakers and microphones
• Camouflage all hardware and cables with non-toxic, bark-matching paint
• Install the accessible post with braille panel, QR code, and hearing loop
• Run 72 hours of continuous system testing to check battery life, speech recognition, speaker direction, and response latency | ☐ | | Recruit and train 15 community “Tree Steward” volunteers to support visitor orientation, collect feedback, and conduct basic weekly equipment checks | ☐ | | Run a 2-week soft launch open only to pre-registered groups (local school classes, senior centers, disability advocacy groups) to collect real-world feedback | ☐ | | Adjust system settings based on soft launch feedback (e.g., increase volume for hard-of-hearing visitors, add requested content topics, re-angle speakers to reduce noise spill) | ☐ | Deliverables Fully installed, camouflaged Talking Tree hardware, trained Tree Steward cohort, soft launch feedback report with all critical adjustments completed, visitor/volunteer quick-reference guide Responsible Parties Installation team, arborist, community coordinator, Tree Steward volunteers, tech team Success Metrics - Zero tree damage (bark scratches, root disturbance, canopy damage) recorded during installation, per post-install arborist check - 72-hour continuous system test passes with zero critical failures - 100% of critical soft launch feedback issues resolved before public opening - Noise levels at nearby paths and residential edges remain ≤55dB during testing Risk Mitigation - Keep replacement hardware parts on-site during installation to avoid delays - Assign an on-call tech support member to resolve system bugs within 2 hours during the soft launch --- Phase 4: Grand Opening & Long-Term Community Stewardship Timeline: Month 11 onwards (ongoing operations) | Actionable Checklist Items | Completed? | |-----------------------------|------------| | Host a free public grand opening event, featuring storytelling from community memory contributors, kids’ nature craft activities, accessibility orientation sessions, and local media outreach | ☐ | | Execute recurring maintenance on a fixed schedule:
• *Weekly*: Tree Stewards conduct visual hardware checks, clear debris from microphones, and collect visitor feedback
• *Quarterly*: Arborist conducts a full tree health check; tech team runs system updates and adds 10 new ecology facts/community stories to the content library; community team hosts a free nature program at the tree (spring bird walk, fall leaf scavenger hunt, etc.)
• *Bi-annually*: Adjust rubber mounting straps to maintain 2cm growth slack; run an accessibility audit with disabled community members; conduct a privacy compliance audit to confirm no unauthorized visitor data is stored
• *Annually*: Replace worn rubber straps; run full battery and hardware diagnostics; publish a public impact report with visitor numbers, feedback, and tree health data | ☐ | | Enforce ongoing privacy and safety protocols:
• Never store or transmit raw visitor audio to cloud servers; all voice processing remains on the local edge unit
• Review all visitor-submitted stories via a 3-person community moderation team before adding them to the memory bank; remove guideline-violating content within 24 hours of a report
• Set operating hours to 8AM–7PM (summer) / 8AM–5PM (winter) to avoid after-hours noise; auto-adjust volume based on ambient noise levels | ☐ | | Roll out iterative upgrades as budget allows:
• Year 2: Add non-invasive soil moisture and air quality sensors so the Tree can share real-time ecosystem updates (e.g., “My roots are nice and damp after last night’s rain!”)
• Year 3: Co-develop a K-5 nature education curriculum with local schools, using the Tree as an outdoor classroom
• Year 4: Add multilingual support for all languages commonly spoken in the surrounding community | ☐ | Deliverables Quarterly public nature programs, annual public impact and tree health reports, regularly updated community content library, iterative accessibility upgrades Responsible Parties Community coordinator, arborist, tech maintenance team, Tree Steward volunteers, content moderation team Success Metrics - ≥12,000 annual visitor interactions with the Tree - Zero signs of tree stress (bark damage, canopy dieback, girdling) at quarterly arborist checks - Post-interaction visitor satisfaction ≥4.6/5, with zero sustained noise or privacy complaints over a 12-month period - 30% of content in the Tree’s memory bank is contributed by community members Risk Mitigation - Install privacy-preserving motion sensors (no facial recognition, no audio recording) to detect equipment vandalism, with instant alerts sent to the maintenance team; build community ownership via the Tree Steward program to reduce vandalism risk - Develop an extreme weather response plan: remotely power down the system 24 hours before forecast high winds, heavy snow, or storms; conduct a full system and tree health check within 24 hours of severe weather passing - Maintain a dedicated annual maintenance budget line to replace hardware as needed, avoiding long periods of system downtime --- Final Cross-Phase Accountability Rule The host tree’s health is the highest project priority at every stage. If the arborist identifies installation-related tree stress at any point, the team will immediately remove all hardware, adjust mounting methods, and only resume work when the tree’s full recovery is confirmed.

title: 老人智能手机使用
text:
Bridging the Digital Divide: Smartphones and the Elderly

In an era defined by unprecedented technological advancement, smartphones have become extensions of ourselves, serving as gateways to information, social connection, and essential services. However, this digital revolution has inadvertently widened the generational gap, leaving many elderly individuals grappling with feelings of exclusion and inadequacy. While smartphones present significant challenges for older adults, embracing their potential and actively supporting the elderly in navigating this digital landscape is crucial for fostering an inclusive society.

The barriers faced by the elderly in adopting smartphones are multifaceted and substantial. Firstly, the complex interface, replete with tiny icons, intricate menus, and rapidly evolving operating systems, can be overwhelmingly intimidating for individuals who did not grow up with such technology. Age-related physical declines, such as diminished eyesight, reduced hearing, and less steady hand movements, further complicate tasks like typing, reading small text, or using touchscreens accurately. Furthermore, the internet is rife with misinformation, scams, and complex privacy settings, posing a genuine threat to seniors who may be less digitally literate and more vulnerable to exploitation. Consequently, many elderly people approach smartphones with apprehension, fearing they will make mistakes or fall victim to fraud. This anxiety can lead to social isolation, as more and more daily activities—from scheduling medical appointments to video-calling family—migrate online. During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, this exclusion became starkly evident when seniors without digital skills struggled to access health codes, order groceries, or maintain vital connections with loved ones.

Despite these challenges, the benefits of smartphones for the elderly are transformative and cannot be ignored. Primarily, these devices serve as lifelines to the outside world, combating the loneliness that often accompanies old age. Through video calls and instant messaging, grandparents can witness their grandchildren grow up daily and maintain meaningful relationships regardless of physical distance. Beyond social connection, smartphones offer unparalleled convenience. Applications for ride-hailing, food delivery, online banking, and telemedicine empower seniors to live more independently, especially those with limited mobility. Moreover, smartphones are portals to lifelong learning and entertainment. Seniors can explore new hobbies through online tutorials, read digital books, listen to their favorite music, or engage in mentally stimulating games, thereby keeping their minds active and engaged. In essence, a smartphone can significantly enhance an older adult’s quality of life, granting them greater autonomy and a stronger sense of belonging in contemporary society.

Addressing the digital divide requires a concerted effort from technology developers, communities, and families. Tech companies must prioritize inclusive design, integrating accessible features such as larger text options, simplified interfaces, voice commands, and robust, easy-to-understand security protections as standard rather than afterthoughts. Community centers and senior organizations can play a vital role by offering patient, hands-on training workshops tailored specifically to the needs and learning paces of older adults. Perhaps most importantly, family members, particularly younger generations, should approach teaching their elders with empathy and patience. Taking the time to walk them through basic functions, setting up helpful accessibility features, and reassuring them about online safety can dramatically boost their confidence.

In conclusion, while smartphones pose undeniable hurdles for the elderly, they also hold the key to greater connectivity, independence, and engagement with the world. Navigating the digital age should not mean leaving our senior citizens behind. By designing more inclusive technology, providing accessible education, and offering patient support, we can empower the elderly to embrace these tools confidently. Ultimately, bridging this digital divide is not merely about teaching technical skills; it is about preserving their dignity, combating isolation, and ensuring that everyone, regardless of age, can participate fully in the digital world.

title: 乡村的变化
text:
Speech: The Countryside Doesn’t Just Grow Crops — It Grows New Dreams
(适合校园、青年论坛、国际文化交流场合，语速适中约8分钟)

Good morning, distinguished guests, dear friends, and fellow young changemakers:

Let me open with a memory from when I was 7 years old. That summer, my mom took me to visit my grandma in her small mountain village in southeast China. I tripped on a rutted mud path within 10 minutes of getting off the rickety long-distance bus, my brand-new white sneakers caked in thick, sticky clay that took three days to scrub off. The outhouse at the end of the yard smelled so bad I held my breath every time I ran there. When the power cut out at 8 p.m., as it did almost every other night, we sat in the sweltering dark fanning ourselves with palm leaves, listening to grandma sigh: “When will our village ever catch up with the city?”

If you asked me to describe that village 18 years ago, the words would come easy: isolation, hardship, a place young people fled as soon as they could. A place where only the elderly and left-behind kids stayed, watching the buses carry the working-age population away to coastal factories. But last Spring Festival, when I drove back to that same village, I almost got lost. Because everything I remembered had changed.

The mud path I tripped on? It is now a smooth two-lane asphalt road, with solar streetlights standing tall along the sides. A public bus stops at the village entrance every hour: it takes seniors to the county hospital for free annual checkups, takes kids to the newly built central primary school with a computer lab and a soccer field, takes crates of local tangerines and bamboo shoots straight to the city’s farmers’ markets. The smelly outhouse? Long gone, replaced by clean flush toilets connected to the village’s new sewage treatment system. The small river that used to be choked with plastic waste and livestock runoff? It runs clear now, with lotus flowers blooming in summer, and wooden camping platforms built along the bank. On weekends, city families drive hours to pitch tents there, pick strawberries at the nearby orchard, and eat wood-fired rice and free-range chicken at family-run homestays.
Take Uncle Li, a neighbor who used to work on an electronics factory assembly line in Guangdong, coming home only once every two years for Spring Festival. Three years ago, he moved back for good, started a farmer cooperative growing organic tangerines on the once-barren hills, and opened a short-video account to livestream his harvests. Last year, his team sold over 3 million yuan worth of fruit, and hired 27 villagers who used to travel a thousand miles for jobs. No more leaving toddlers with grandparents, no more missing kids’ high school graduations to earn a paycheck.

But let me tell you: the biggest, most profound change is not the paved roads, not the new brick houses, not the 5G signal that now reaches even the highest hilltop. It is the shift in how people see the village itself.
When I was little, every parent in the village told their kids the same thing: “Study hard, get into a good college, move to the city, and never come back.” Staying in the village meant you were a failure, that you had no ambition. Today? I have met 24-year-old Xiaoyu, who came back after graduating from agricultural university, teaching villagers to grow high-value medicinal herbs instead of low-profit, labor-intensive rice. I have met A-Mei, a Miao ethnic embroidery artist, who runs a workshop teaching left-behind women to stitch traditional patterns onto tote bags and silk scarves, selling their work to customers across 12 countries online. I have sat in on a village council meeting, where grandfathers in cloth shoes, young returned entrepreneurs, and college student volunteers sat around a wooden table arguing for an hour about where to build the new public basketball court, how to split tourism profits fairly between households, and why they should protect the 200-year-old banyan tree at the village center instead of cutting it down to build more parking spots.
The village is no longer a place people run from. It is a place people come back to: to build, to create, to belong.

Now, I am not here to paint you an unrealistic picture of perfect rural paradise. We still have remote hamlets where roads get cut off by heavy snow in winter. We still face shortages of qualified teachers and general practitioners in many rural areas. We still watch precious old traditions—from hand papermaking to folk opera—fading as the older generation passes on. These are gaps we still have to fill, hard work we still have ahead.
But let us stop and ask: what does a “good countryside” even mean? It does not mean copying skyscrapers and chain stores from cities, erasing every trace of our rural roots to chase some narrow idea of “development”. It means a place where the air is clean, the water is drinkable, and you can earn a decent living without having to leave your family behind. It means a place where kids can get a quality education, elders can get medical care without traveling for hours, and the old trees, old recipes, old festival rituals are still there for all of us to come home to.

And this change does not happen by accident. It does not come from government documents alone, or from one-time charity donations. It comes from the road worker who spent three months digging through mountain rock to lay the first stretch of asphalt. It comes from the young entrepreneur who takes a risk to come home and start a farm, even when their own parents say they are throwing away a good city job. It comes from the primary school teacher who stayed in the village for 32 years, teaching three generations of kids to read.
It can even come from you. It comes from the college student who spends a summer teaching art and science to village kids. It comes from the designer who helps local farmers create beautiful, practical packaging for their honey and tea so they can sell their products for a fair price. It comes from the traveler who chooses to stay at a village homestay instead of an international chain hotel, who listens to the old villagers tell their stories instead of just taking photos for social media. It comes from every person who refuses to see the countryside as a “backward place to be fixed”, and instead sees it as a living, breathing part of who we are—worth caring for, worth investing in, worth fighting for.

Last time I visited grandma, she was sitting in her small courtyard under the loquat tree she planted 40 years ago, scrolling short videos on her 5G phone to learn a new recipe for pickled radish. She looked up at me and smiled: “When I was young, I thought the best life was living in a tall city apartment with an elevator. Now? All my city cousins call me every week, asking if they can come stay in my yard for summer vacation, to eat homegrown tomatoes and listen to the cicadas.”

That, to me, is the magic of all these changes. The countryside is not “catching up” to the city. It is becoming its own best self: a place that holds our oldest, warmest memories, and makes space for our newest, boldest dreams. It does not just grow crops. It grows opportunities. It grows connections. It grows home.
And we all get to be part of that growth.

Thank you.

title: 青春与梦想
text:
The Lanterns Tucked in Our Cuffs
*A prose on youth and dreams*

Youth does not announce itself with a fanfare.
It leaks in through the cracked window of a third-floor classroom, tangles in chalk dust and dandelion fluff caught on bicycle spokes, and fizzes, half-warm, in the dented orange soda bottle tucked under a desk. It tastes like cherry popsicle dripped on a uniform collar, sounds like off-key singing of teenagers pedaling home against the sunset, and glows, soft and unruly, like fireflies bobbing above summer clover.

We did not call them dreams back then.
They were half-scrawled verses in the margin of a math workbook, silly glowing bargains we whispered to fireflies trapped in mason jars, quiet daydreams that turned the monotonous dribble of a basketball on asphalt into a drumbeat marching somewhere far, far away. We wanted to chase storm clouds for a living, write biographies for stray cats, open a corner shop that sold nothing but old jazz records and iced lemon tea. These were not goals, not five-year plans, not bullet points on a resume. They were tiny breathing things we cupped in our palms: fragile as dandelion fluff, bright as shards of a fallen star.

Grown-ups called it naivety. They tapped our report cards and spoke of practical paths, steady paychecks, roots sunk deep in sensible soil. But we tucked those glowing nothings into the cuffs of our oversized school uniforms anyway: stolen starlight, secret lanterns no one else was allowed to see.

Years later, the uniforms fray at the collars and end up in donation bins. The bicycle rusts by the stairwell, and the firefly jars cracked long ago, their tiny embers spilled back into the summer dark. Some of our lanterns sputtered out in the cold rain of rent bills and tight deadlines, of awkward entry-level interviews and quiet compromises we never saw coming. Some shrank, soft and unassuming: from *“I will change the world”* to *“I will make it through this week”*; from wandering every continent on a sailboat to tending a windowsill of succulents that actually stay alive.

But here is the secret no one tells you when you lean against the school fence at dusk, sticky with popsicle juice:
Youth is not a chapter glued shut in a yearbook. It is the habit of tucking light into your cuffs.

It is the split second on a gray crowded subway commute when you still glance up at bloated summer clouds and think, *what if*? It is the off-key pop song you hummed at 17 that still slips out while you wash dishes after work. It is the way you pause, late for dinner and laden with grocery bags, to watch a single firefly flicker above a city flowerbed.

Dreams do not have to be towering mountains to conquer. They can be tiny, stubborn embers that keep your steps light when the road feels long. They are proof that we once carried whole summer skies in our chests — unapologetic, unhurried, unafraid to glow.

So do not brush the starlight off your cuffs.
The 17-year-old in scuffed sneakers with a jar full of fireflies is still walking beside you. And every time you dare to want something soft, something bright, something entirely your own?
That is youth, breathing.
That is the dream, glowing still.

---

 参考译文：《袖底灯火》
青春从不会大张旗鼓地登场。
它从三楼教室开裂的窗缝溜进来，缠在粉笔灰与自行车辐条挂着的蒲公英绒上，在桌肚那瓶磕出凹痕、温乎乎的橘子汽水里滋滋冒泡。它是校服领口樱桃冰棒的甜，是少年们迎着落日蹬车时跑调的歌，是夏日三叶草丛上空浮荡的萤火虫，软乎乎的，偏带着点不服管束的亮。

那时候我们不管这叫梦想。
它们是数学练习册页边写了半行的碎诗，是对着梅森罐里的萤火虫小声许下的、亮晶晶的傻约定，是走神时的遐想——把沥青操场上篮球单调的咚咚声，都听成了奔赴远方的鼓点。我们想靠追积雨云谋生，想给流浪猫写传记，想开家街角小店，只卖老爵士唱片和冰柠檬茶。这些不是目标，不是五年规划，更不是简历上的光鲜条目。它们是捧在手心会呼吸的小生命：和蒲公英绒一样轻软，和落星碎片一样透亮。

大人们说这是天真。他们敲敲我们的成绩单，念叨着要走务实的路，拿稳定的薪水，在稳妥的土壤里扎根。可我们还是把这些亮闪闪的“无用心事”，塞进了宽大校服的袖管里：那是偷来的星光，是不许旁人窥见的秘密灯火。

许多年后，校服领口磨破，最终被放进捐赠箱；自行车在楼梯间锈住，装萤火虫的玻璃罐早裂了缝，那些细碎的光都漏回了夏夜的风里。有些袖中灯火被冷雨打湿：房租账单、赶工的死线、青涩的求职面试、还有那些从没料到的沉默妥协，噼啪几声，就暗了下去。还有些缩得小小的，温和平实：从前喊着要改变世界，后来只盼能好好撑过这一周；从前想驾帆船走遍大洲，后来只愿窗台上的多肉能一盆盆好好活下去。

可当你黄昏靠在学校围栏上、满手冰棒黏汁的时候，没人会告诉你这个秘密：
青春从不是毕业纪念册里粘死的某一章节，它是一种总往袖底藏一点光的习惯。

它是你挤在灰扑扑的通勤地铁里，抬头望见蓬软的夏云时，忽然闪过的那一秒“万一呢”；是你十七岁跑调哼过的流行歌，下班洗碗时仍会不自觉溜到嘴边；是你拎着满袋食材、赶晚饭都要迟了，仍会停下脚步，望一望城市花坛上空那只忽明忽暗的萤火虫。

梦想不必非是等着人征服的崇山峻岭。它可以是细小又倔强的余烬，在路仿佛走不到头的时候，让你的脚步仍能轻捷几分。它证明着我们也曾把一整幅夏夜星空揣在胸口——理直气壮，不慌不忙，敢发光，也敢张扬。

所以别掸掉袖口的星光。
那个穿磨边球鞋、揣着满罐萤火虫的十七岁少年，从来都走在你身旁。
而每一次你敢去向往一点柔软的、明亮的、完完全全属于你的东西时——
那就是青春在呼吸。
那就是梦想，仍在发光。

title: 海边的灯塔
text:
Step-by-Step Practical Guide to Coastal Lighthouse Visits
Standing sentinel over rocky shorelines, shipping lanes, and churning surf, coastal lighthouses blend working maritime infrastructure, centuries of human drama, and some of the most dramatic coastal views on the planet. This no-fluff guide is designed for day trippers, photographers, history buffs, and casual explorers to visit safely, respectfully, and get the most out of your trip, whether you are heading to a remote tidal-island beacon or a popular cliffside heritage site.

---

 Step 1: Pre-Visit Planning (Avoid Wasted Trips & Preventable Risks)
Complete these checks before you leave home to skip common pitfalls:
- Verify access rules from official sources first: Skip generic map app listings—cross-check information from the site’s operator (national parks, national trusts, coast guard auxiliaries, or local lighthouse preservation societies) for three non-negotiable details:
  1. Actual opening hours: Many small, volunteer-run lighthouses have irregular seasonal hours and may close last minute for storm damage or staff shortages.
  2. Access type: Confirm if the site is reachable via paved road, clifftop trail, or tidal causeway (a path fully submerged at high tide).
  3. Restrictions: Note if tower climbs require timed advance tickets, if pets/drones are banned, and if any zones are closed for seabird nesting, cliff erosion, or active coast guard operations.
- Double-check critical environmental forecasts:
  1. Tide charts (for causeway-access sites: build a 1-hour safety buffer on either side of low tide to avoid stranding; never attempt to cross a flooding causeway—tidal currents can sweep cars and people away in minutes).
  2. Marine weather: Cancel trips if thunderstorms, gale-force wind gusts, or dense fog advisories are posted. Lighthouses are exposed high points at extreme risk of lightning strikes, and lantern-deck wind gusts can hit 50+ mph even on seemingly mild days.
- Pack site-specific gear: Wear closed-toe, non-slip hiking shoes (rocks and metal spiral stairs are slick with sea spray and algae), bring a windproof/waterproof outer layer (coastal temperatures can drop 10–15°F/5–8°C in minutes), reef-safe waterproof sunscreen, a headlamp (for sunrise/sunset visits when trails go dark after hours), binoculars (for spotting seabirds, seals, and passing ships), and basic first-aid supplies for scrapes from sharp rock. Note: Nearly all historic lighthouses have no elevators, with 50–150 narrow spiral stairs to the top—plan accordingly if you have claustrophobia or limited mobility.

 Step 2: Safe Arrival & Site Entry
Follow these rules as you arrive to avoid accidents and fines:
- Arrive early in peak season: Most lighthouses have only 10–20 parking spots; aim to arrive within 1 hour of sunrise to skip crowds, access the best photo light, and beat harsh midday winds.
- Stay strictly on marked paths: Unmarked cliff edges around lighthouses are often severely eroded and can collapse without warning. Avoid walking on algae-covered intertidal rocks—they are as slick as ice, and rogue waves can sweep people off exposed outcrops even on calm days.
- Review on-site notice boards before exploring: Look for posted warnings about nesting seabird zones (where even small disturbances can cause parent birds to abandon chicks), temporary trail closures, or scheduled fog signal tests. If you brought a drone, confirm no-flight rules: most active lighthouses sit under coast guard flight paths, and drone disruptions to navigation can carry thousands of dollars in fines.
- Never tamper with active navigation equipment: At working lighthouses, beacons, AIS (Automatic Identification System) antennas, and fog signals are critical for guiding ships; tampering can lead to maritime accidents and criminal charges.

 Step 3: Tower Climb & On-Site Etiquette
Stick to these guidelines to keep yourself, other visitors, and historic assets safe:
- Follow spiral stair protocol: Narrow stone/metal stairs only fit one person in most spots; stay to the right to let descending visitors pass, hold the handrail at all times (note: tower tops sway slightly in high winds—this is intentional, engineered flexibility to survive storms, not a structural failure), and never stop mid-staircase to take photos, which creates dangerous bottlenecks.
- Protect the historic lens: When you reach the lantern room, never touch the Fresnel lens—these 19th-century prismatic glass pieces are often irreplaceable artifacts, and oil from fingertips can etch permanent damage into glass coatings. Avoid staring directly at the beacon if it activates during low visibility; the light is intense enough to cause temporary eye damage. If a fog signal activates while you are inside the tower, cover your ears—the 120+ decibel horn can cause permanent hearing damage at close range.
- Practice respectful shoreline behavior: Keep at least 50 yards (46 meters) of distance from seals, sea lions, and nesting seabirds; never feed wildlife, pack out all trash (including food scraps that disrupt coastal ecosystems), and avoid carving or marking stone walls or tower surfaces. Keep dogs on short, fixed leashes at all times, and stay out of closed habitat restoration zones.

 Step 4: Maximize Your Visit (Beyond Quick Photos)
Use these tips to turn a 20-minute photo stop into a memorable experience:
- Time your visit for optimal conditions: For quiet views and striking photos, arrive 30 minutes before sunrise, during golden hour before sunset, or in the blue hour after dark when the beacon rotates (bring a tripod for long-exposure shots of light trails and silky surf). *Never* use bright flash, laser pointers, or portable floodlights pointed toward shipping lanes—these can be mistaken for navigation signals and put vessels at risk.
- Seek out insider knowledge: Chat with on-site docents or volunteer keepers—most have deep expertise in local shipwrecks, former keepers’ grueling daily routines, regional coastal lore, and hidden nearby tide pools. Many sites run public demonstrations of historic fog horns, lens rotation mechanisms, or keeper-era cooking demonstrations on weekends.
- Collect meaningful mementos: Stop by the small on-site gift shop (proceeds almost always go directly to lighthouse restoration and maintenance) for site-specific patches, commemorative passport stamps, or local maritime history books, rather than generic mass-produced coastal souvenirs. For longer trips, ask about volunteer keeper programs, which let you stay on-site for a few days in exchange for helping with tours, maintenance, and groundskeeping.
- Know when to seek shelter: If you hear the fog signal activate unexpectedly, notice rapidly thickening sea fog, or feel wind speeds pick up sharply, cut your exploration short and head back to your vehicle—coastal fog can reduce visibility to zero in under 10 minutes, making cliffside trails nearly impossible to navigate.

 Step 5: Post-Visit Safety & Stewardship
Wrap up your trip responsibly to protect the site for future visitors:
- Stick to your timeline: If you accessed the lighthouse via a tidal causeway, start your return trip 30 minutes before the published high-tide cutoff; never attempt to wade or drive through moving tidal water, which rises faster than a person can walk and carries powerful undercurrents. For evening visits, use your headlamp on the trail and watch for loose gravel and uneven rock.
- Follow Leave No Trace rules: Pack out all waste, including fruit peels, tissue, and discarded fishing line you find on the trail. Never take rocks, shells, or historic artifacts (like old glass or metal hardware from lighthouse grounds) as souvenirs—these are protected parts of the coastal and historic ecosystem.
- Report hazards to site managers: If you spot loose railings, eroded trail sections, or injured wildlife on your way out, alert a docent or send a quick note to the site’s preservation society—most small lighthouses operate with tiny volunteer teams and may not catch hazards immediately.
- Support long-term preservation: 70% of historic U.S. coastal lighthouses, and nearly half of European heritage lighthouses, receive no ongoing government funding and rely entirely on visitor donations and volunteer labor. Even a $5 donation helps cover lens maintenance, trail repairs, and accessibility upgrades. If you share photos from your trip, tag the local lighthouse preservation group to help spread the word about their work.

---

 Quick Emergency Cheat Sheet
- If stranded by rising tide: Climb to the highest available solid ground, call local coastal emergency services or the coast guard immediately, and never attempt to swim or wade across floodwater.
- If approached by defensive wildlife (protective seals, dive-bombing nesting seabirds): Back away slowly, do not run, and put a large rock or trail marker between you and the animal.
- If lightning or severe wind hits mid-visit: Move away from the lighthouse tower and exposed cliff edges, take shelter in a hard-roofed vehicle or solid visitor center, and avoid standing under isolated trees.

title: 家乡的春节
text:
The Spring Festival of My Hometown
*A Familiar Reverie, in the manner of the old English essayists*

When the last amber persimmon has dropped from the gnarled bough at the lane’s end, and the frost has bleached cottage thatch to the hue of weathered parchment, a soft expectant hush falls upon my rural thorp. The fields lie fallow, the ploughs are stacked by byre walls, and even the sheep huddle close in the fold, as if the whole countryside has drawn breath, waiting for the first glad signal of Spring Festival. Wintersweet bushes by cottage doors swell with bud, and on mild mid-days their honeyed, sharp scent steals through every crack of lattice, as if the earth itself were breathing out promises of warmth to come.

The preparations creep on gently, as all rural rites do—no hurry or blare about them. On an appointed day every goodwife flings her door wide to the crisp air, wielding bamboo brooms to brush a year’s soot and chaff from the rafters, beating dust from quilts till the yard glows with floating down. It is no mere housekeeping, this: they sweep out the petty vexations of the bygone year, too—the failed turnip crop, the broken teacup, the cross words spoken over a tired harvest supper—to leave clean corners for good luck to nest in. The creak of stone mills hums through the lanes thereafter, as women grind soybeans for silken tofu; steam curls in thick plumes from kitchen vents, where grandmothers tend great iron pots, steaming dense loaves of glutinous rice cake sweetened with dried osmanthus. *Nian gao*, they call it: a soft homely pun for “rising higher each year”, a wish no grand poet could better, rooted as it is in the farmer’s quiet hope for taller grain, fuller baskets, kinder seasons.

By the week’s end, the village schoolmaster has set his deal table beneath the old oak at the crossroads, his inkstone heaped with jet-black ink, a stack of cinnabar-red paper at his elbow. He is the only man for miles with a clerkly hand, and husbandmen drift to him one by one, bearing their finished couplets home as tenderly as if they held loose pages of Virgil. Many a stalwart ploughman, for all his sureness with plough and flail, will paste his scrolls crooked on the doorposts, and bear his wife’s laughing scold with a sheepish grin, vowing to mend his care next year—a vow as often renewed, I dare say, as it is broken. Pine boughs are nailed above lintels for luck, their dark green defying the frost; and on market day the lanes throng with baskets of amber stove-sugar, blown into hollow little melons that crackle between the teeth. These are for the Kitchen God, you must know, that he may carry none but sweet reports of the household to the celestial court. I have always thought it the most amiable of pious frauds: even the dwellers in heaven, it seems, are not above a little well-meant bribery, if it makes the year kinder to plain folk.

New Year’s Eve draws in soft and blue at the edges, with wood smoke curling low over the roofs. The first squibs sputter at the lane corners as dusk falls, their sharp sulphur tang winding through the scent of braised pork and steamed dumplings. Children dart between doorways in wadded coats, their cheeks bright as hawthorn berries, their pockets bulging with peanuts and lumps of sugar, while elders settle in the warm inglenook beside the stove, shelling sunflower seeds and recounting tales of harsh winters and bountiful harvests, of weddings and births and neighbours long gone to their rest. Red lanterns are strung between peach boughs in every yard, glowing like fallen moons caught in the bare twigs; no one hurries to bed on this night, for to keep watch till midnight is to “guard the year”—to hold fast to the old days while welcoming the new. When the clock at last strikes twelve, a thousand firecrackers roar out across the fields at once, and the dark sky blazes with fitful crimson, as if all the wild poppies of June had been plucked and scattered across the winter firmament. The sound rolls over fallow rice paddies and turnip patches, bouncing off the distant hills, as loud and glad as any village peal of bells.

New Year’s morning breaks clear and crisp, the frost lying thin as powdered sugar on the stubble. Every soul dons their best attire: boys in navy cotton coats stitched thick against the cold, girls with scarlet ribbons braided into their black hair, elders with fur caps pulled low against the wind. They file along the raised field balks in little groups, tramping from cottage to cottage to bow and give greeting, their boots crunching on the frozen ruts. At every door they are pressed with tea and candies and handfuls of roasted melon seeds; the children bow low to the grey-haired grandfathers and grandmothers, who tuck small scarlet envelopes into their mittened palms, holding a few bright coins “to pin down the years”. I used to think it meant pinning down time, keeping the old year from slipping away too fast; now I fancy it is rather joy they pin—small, warm, tangible joy, safe in a child’s closed fist.

It is many a long year since I trod those frost-hard lanes at New Year. I have sat by polished marble hearths in great cities, and feasted on dishes dressed with all the art of famous cooks; I have watched grand fireworks burst over steeples and crowded squares. Yet none of these fine things ever carried half the sweetness of my grandmother’s osmanthus rice cake, half the warmth of that smouldering stove corner, half the bright wonder of those winking red lanterns strung between bare peach boughs. The city keeps its feasts with noise and parade, but the country keeps Spring Festival like a secret shared between neighbours, a quiet promise passed from hand to hand.

For this is no mere holiday marked on a printed calendar, you see. It is the farming year’s soft turning point: the moment when the dormant seed stirs a little beneath the frost, when scattered children trudge home from distant towns, when even the poorest cottage has a stick of sugar to offer a stranger, a patch of red on its door to fend off the dark. It is spring before the spring comes: hope made visible, sweet on the tongue, warm in the palm.
Somewhere, even now, I think I can smell it on the wind: the honeyed tang of wintersweet, the sharp reek of gunpowder, the warm steam of rice cake drifting over the fields. The thorp will be hushing now, waiting. It is the Spring Festival of home, and it stays in the blood long after the last lantern has guttered out, long after the last echo of firecrackers has died away over the fallow fields.

---
 创作说明
本文以查尔斯·兰姆《伊利亚随笔》的温厚絮语调性为核心，借鉴吉尔伯特·怀特《塞耳彭自然史》的乡村物候书写传统：
1. 用英式随笔特有的与假想读者闲谈的口吻（`I dare say`/`you must know`）替代激昂抒情，所有年俗（掸尘、蒸年糕、祭灶、守岁、拜年、压岁钱）均融入农耕生活细节，不作生硬的文化注解；
2. 以维吉尔牧歌、乡野钟声、六月虞美人、壁炉暖角等西方读者熟悉的田园意象互文中式年俗，既保留东方乡愁内核，也贴合古典英国散文的人文质感；
3. 节奏舒缓绵长，以岁暮物候起、以余味忆旧收，契合英式小品“微物中见恒常”的抒情逻辑。

title: 冬天里的小麻雀
text:
Fragile Flames in the Frost: A Literary Appreciation of the Winter Sparrow Across Prose and Poetry
 Abstract
Winter has long been framed in global literary tradition as a season of desolation, existential stillness, and sublime, unforgiving cold—a backdrop for heroic endurance, tragic isolation, or meditations on mortality. Overlooked in this grand narrative of frost and silence is the humble house sparrow (*Passer domesticus*): a small, unglamorous resident bird that never migrates, never boasts brilliant plumage or lyrical song, and lives at the porous, unmarked edge between wild nature and human settlement. This essay traces the literary figure of the winter sparrow across three distinct, cross-cultural textual traditions: Emily Dickinson’s 19th-century lyric poetry, where the sparrow perching on snow-laden boughs embodies a quiet, unassuming divinity rooted in ordinary life; Lao She’s 1937 novel *Rickshaw Boy*, where flocks of sparrows huddling in the frozen alleys of Beiping mirror the uncelebrated, gritty resilience of working-class people surviving structural hardship; and Terry Tempest Williams’ 21st-century nature writing, where winter sparrows become a metaphor for fragile, reciprocal connection between humans and the nonhuman world amid accelerating climate crisis. Across these texts, the winter sparrow emerges not as a symbol of grand heroism or romantic transcendence, but as a “fragile flame in the frost”: a small, shivering, stubbornly alive presence that anchors readers to the tangible, unglamorous warmth that sustains life through the longest cold.
---
 Critical Appreciation
Literary winters are rarely kind to small, unassuming things. From the howling heath where King Lear rages against the storm to the frozen mountains of classical Chinese poetry where “a thousand mountains hold no trace of bird flight,” winter is staged as a theater of the sublime: a force that dwarfs the individual, strips the world of ornament, and demands feats of courage or endurance from those who would outlast it. In this landscape of grand, icy drama, the sparrow is an easy afterthought. Derided in common idiom across languages as a feathered pest of small brain and smaller worth—too common to merit poetic tribute, too scrappy to carry noble symbolic weight—it flits at the edges of canonical winter scenes, chasing crumbs, huddling from wind, making thin, unmusical chirps that rarely make it into the official record of the season. Yet it is precisely this lack of grandeur that makes the winter sparrow one of the most quietly powerful emblems of resilience in world literature. It does not fight the frost. It does not outfly the winter. It simply stays, and lives, and in that quiet persistence, cuts through the cold of even the harshest literary landscapes.
For Emily Dickinson, who spent most of her adult life in the frost-prone hills of Amherst, Massachusetts, the winter sparrow was a deliberate rebuke to the romantic tradition of celebratory, high-flying songbirds. Where Percy Shelley framed the skylark as a “blithe Spirit” soaring above the clouds to pour forth transcendent verse, Dickinson turned her gaze to the small, brown birds that landed on her window ledge in the depths of January, fluffed against the cold, waiting for crumbs of bread she left out for them. In an untitled 1873 lyric, she writes: “The Sparrow’s chirp from leafless boughs / Outweighs a choral psalm: / He wears no robe, he reads no rite, / But living is his palm.” For Dickinson, the sparrow’s sanctity came not from distance from the mortal world, but from its unapologetic embeddedness in it. It did not fly south to avoid the snow; it perched on bare branches, its feet clinging to ice-crusted wood, and sang not for an audience of poets, but for no audience at all. It did not perform faith through grand ritual; it practiced faith simply by surviving the night, by waking to chirp when the sun rose, even when the temperature dropped well below freezing. In a body of work preoccupied with finding the divine in the overlooked, the winter sparrow was Dickinson’s smallest, most perfect prophet: proof that holiness did not reside in cathedrals or epic poetry, but in the shivering, unglamorous persistence of a life too small to be noticed by the grand world.
Half a world away, in the frozen alleyways of 1930s Beiping, Lao She populated his novel *Rickshaw Boy* with winter sparrows that carried a different, no less sacred weight: the weight of shared, uncelebrated survival. The novel’s protagonist, Xiangzi, is a young rickshaw puller who battles wind, frost, poverty, and exploitation to eke out a living in the city’s brutal winters, where the north wind “scoured rutted streets until the frozen earth cracked like old pottery,” as Howard Goldblatt translates the text. In these passages, the sparrows are not decorative metaphors or spiritual symbols; they are Xiangzi’s fellow survivors. Lao She describes them fluffed into round gray balls, huddled in the sun-warmed lee of compound walls, darting out to snatch crumbs of roasted sweet potato before the cold could stiffen their wings, never flying far even when chased by passersby, because the wind outside the wall was too cruel to bear. There is no romance to these sparrows: they are scrappy, hungry, sometimes so cold they can barely chirp, and they will fight each other for a single crumb if they have to. But they are alive, just as Xiangzi is alive, even when the world seems designed to freeze him out. Unlike the mythic heroes of traditional winter tales, neither Xiangzi nor the sparrows aspire to conquer the cold or transcend their circumstances. They only aspire to get through the day: to find a bite to eat, a spot of sun, a moment out of the wind. In writing these small birds into the margins of Xiangzi’s story, Lao She refuses the grand narrative of winter as a test of individual heroism. He reminds readers that most people who survive hard winters do not do so with grand speeches or dramatic feats. They do so the way sparrows do: one small hop, one crumb, one sun-warmed minute at a time.
In contemporary nature writing, Terry Tempest Williams extends this lineage of the winter sparrow to frame the bird as a quiet call to ecological connection. Writing from her home in the high desert of Utah, where winter temperatures can drop to minus twenty degrees Fahrenheit and blizzards can bury the landscape for weeks at a time, Williams describes the small flocks of house sparrows that gather on her porch rail through the coldest months. She notes, in *When Women Were Birds*, that a single sparrow weighs barely an ounce, its heart beating 800 times a minute; an unprotected human would die of exposure in the same conditions the sparrow survives through the night, huddled shoulder to shoulder with other sparrows to share body heat, their feathers puffed into tiny insulation layers. For Williams, the winter sparrow is a rebuke to the grand, detached narratives of climate crisis that frame environmental action as a battle to save a distant, abstract planet. The sparrow is close: it sits on her rail, tilts its head when she brings out sunflower seeds, trusts her not to harm it. Surviving the winter, for Williams, is not an individual feat, for sparrows or for humans. It is a practice of mutual care: the sparrows share warmth with each other on the branch, she leaves out seeds for them, and in that small exchange, a fragile bond is formed across species lines. In an era when winters grow more erratic, when unseasonable blizzards and warm spells threaten the small birds’ food supplies and nesting sites, the sparrow’s presence is a reminder that resilience is not about being tough enough to face the cold alone. It is about showing up for the small, vulnerable lives that share the cold with you.
Across all these texts, the winter sparrow’s power lies in its refusal to be sublime. It will never be an eagle, soaring above the storm to symbolize power. It will never be a swan, gliding over frozen lakes to symbolize grace. It will never be a nightingale, singing through the dark to symbolize romantic genius. It will always be a little scruffy, a little hungry, a little too quick to dart away when a shadow passes. But that is precisely why it resonates so deeply across time and culture. For every reader who has ever felt small, unremarkable, and ill-equipped to face the long cold of personal or collective hardship—the cold of grief, of poverty, of isolation, of a world that seems increasingly harsh and unforgiving—the winter sparrow offers a quiet, unpretentious kind of hope. You do not need to fly south to escape the winter. You do not need to sing a perfect song to be worthy of notice. You only need to fluff your feathers against the wind, huddle close to the others who share your wall, take the crumb that is offered, and chirp, even when your throat is cold.
That is the fragile flame the sparrow carries in the frost: not a roaring bonfire that lights up the whole sky, but a tiny, steady warmth, held close to the body, passed from one small bird to the next. It is easy to miss, if you are only looking for grand, blazing miracles. But if you stop, and listen, and look closely at the snow under the bare branches, you will see its tiny footprints, proof that even in the coldest, quietest winter, life persists, unglamorous and unbeatable, one small hop at a time.
---
 References
1.  Dickinson, Emily. *The Poems of Emily Dickinson: Reading Edition*. Edited by R. W. Franklin, Harvard University Press, 1999.
2.  Fudge, Erica. *Animal*. Reaktion Books, 2002. (Critical reference on the cultural status of "common" companion animals in literary representation)
3.  Lao, She. *Rickshaw Boy*. Translated by Howard Goldblatt, Harper Perennial, 2010.
4.  Williams, Terry Tempest. *When Women Were Birds: Fifty-four Variations on Voice*. Picador, 2012.

title: 红楼梦
text:
The Flower Burial
(Adapted from Cao Xueqin’s *A Dream of Red Mansions*, ~500 words)

In the gilded Grand View Garden of the declining Jia noble clan, late spring draped winding painted corridors in drifts of peach and pomegranate petals. Lin Daiyu, the sharp-witted, fragile orphaned cousin taken in by the household, slipped out at dawn with a tiny willow hoe slung over her shoulder, a silk gauze pouch tied to its handle, and a soft broom tucked under her arm. Still stinging from a petty quarrel with the family’s beloved heir Jia Baoyu the night before, she could not bear to see delicate blooms trampled under servants’ rough shoes or swept into muddy, garbage-choked gutters.

She knelt by a low earthen mound beneath an old peach tree, brushing unblemished petals into her pouch one by one, and sang a soft, mournful verse as she worked:
*Men mock my folly as I lay the blooms to rest;*
*Who’ll bury me when my own breath is pressed?*
*Pure they come, and pure they shall return,*
*Not sunk in filth, nor left to fade and burn.*

Hidden beyond a jagged rock slope at her back, Baoyu had been gathering fallen petals in the wide fold of his indigo silk robe. When the lines drifted to his ears, he burst into quiet, heaving sobs, his whole armful of blossoms spilling down the grassy slope. He had long ached with the quiet fear that all beauty fades: that the chattering, bright girls of the garden would one day marry away to distant households, that the family’s gilded fortune would crumble to dust, that Daiyu, light and fragile as a dewdrop on a petal, would not stay by his side forever.

Daiyu turned at the sound, her own eyes red-rimmed from crying. She made to turn and leave, but Baoyu stumbled after her, his robe dusted with pale yellow pollen. “I did not come to tease you,” he said quickly, softly. “I brought petals too. I thought… if they float down the garden stream, they pass the kitchen drains and get soiled with dirty dishwater. Burying them here, where they melt back into clean earth, is far kinder.”

Daiyu’s cold frown softened. Together they piled the last of the blooms into the mound and patted the dark earth smooth over them. A gust of wind shook the peach tree overhead, sending a flurry of petals swirling over both their heads. Baoyu lifted a hand to brush a blossom caught on her ink-black fringe, then drew back halfway, shy and earnest. “When the time comes,” he whispered, “I will bury you too, properly. I will never let you fall into the mud.”

Daiyu’s throat tightened. She tapped his arm lightly with her hoe handle, but spoke no sharp, teasing reply. Far off, her maid’s voice called her name through trailing willow branches. They stood a moment longer, watching the last pale petals drift down to settle on the earthen mound, neither speaking of the quiet, unkeepable promise hanging soft as spring mist over the little flower grave.

title: 故乡的河
text:
说明
这篇读后感围绕语文教材中常选的、作家迟子建的经典散文《故乡的河》(*The River of My Hometown*) 创作，结构包含阅读场景引入、文本细节解读、个人情感共鸣与主旨升华，语言自然流畅，既贴合散文的抒情特质，也适合作为文学课作业、读书分享材料使用。如果您需要对应其他作者的同名作品，可以随时告诉我调整内容。

---

 Reflections on *The River of My Hometown* by Chi Zijian
I first picked up Chi Zijian’s lyrical essay on a gray, rain-dappled weekday in Shanghai, leaning against the concrete embankment of Suzhou Creek as polished tour boats glided past, their speakers blaring scripted introductions of the city’s curated waterside history. The creek, tamed, landscaped, stripped of the wild mudflats and reed thickets that once lined its banks, felt less like a living waterway than a glossy museum exhibit — and that was exactly why Chi’s words hit me like a cool, unplanned splash of unfiltered river water straight to the face.

Chi, the award-winning Heilongjiang-born writer whose work is stitched through with the cold pine scent and vast, snow-dusted skies of China’s far northeast, does not write of her hometown river — the Emur River, which curls through the Arctic Village where she grew up — as a postcard-perfect tourist landmark. She writes of it as a breathing, unruly, beloved member of her small community. She recalls the thunderous crack of breaking ice in late April, when spring thaws send jagged floes grinding down the current so loud villagers would gather on the banks just to listen, as if cheering for a long-lost friend returning home. She describes the slow, sun-warmed shallows of summer where she waded barefoot at seven, her toes sinking into soft silt as her grandfather cast his fishing net, his old canvas jacket smelling of pipe tobacco and riverweed. She writes of the frozen, rock-solid expanse of winter, when the river became the village’s busiest road: sleds loaded with firewood slid across its surface, children chased each other on skates until their eyelashes frosted white, housewives knelt on chipped wooden stools to scrub laundry through holes chopped in the ice, their soapy hands bright red with cold. She never romanticizes the river, either: she remembers the summer flood that rose high enough to swallow riverside vegetable patches, sweep away a neighbor’s chicken coop, and leave caked mud two feet up the walls of low cottages; she remembers the quiet grief of scattering her grandfather’s ashes into the current years later, watching the grey dust dissolve into the moving water until no trace remained.

What lifts this essay far above generic nostalgic writing and makes it feel like a warm, quiet hand pressed to your chest is Chi’s unflinching observation: a hometown river is never just a mix of water, silt, and current. It is the only unedited archive of a place, the one witness that never lies. Old cottages get bulldozed and rebuilt as glass-walled homestays for tourists; lifelong neighbors pass away or move south for better jobs; even the gnarled old willow that once arched over the village’s best swimming hole might be cut down to make room for a paid parking lot. But the river keeps running. It holds the echo of every child’s cackle that bounced off its ripples, every tear a grieving person dropped into its flow, every rusted fishing hook snagged on its rocky bed, every crumpled paper boat a seven-year-old set sailing for the ocean, every quiet secret mumbled to its surface on evenings when the rest of the world was too busy to listen. When Chi writes that even after decades living in Harbin, after standing on the banks of world-famous waterways — the churning Yellow River, the wind-rippled Volga, the Seine glinting under Parisian streetlights — she can still identify the exact, earthy scent of the Emur River the second she steps within ten feet of its banks, I felt a sharp, soft tug of recognition.

I grew up in a small town in southern Zhejiang, where a narrow, jade-green river curled right behind my grandmother’s tile-roofed house. For years, I wrote off my childhood memories of that river as rose-tinted nostalgia: I remembered wading in its shallows to catch pin-thin transparent shrimp in mason jars, skipping flat slate stones across its sun-dappled surface, perching on its rough stone steps to eat mung bean popsicles while summer thunderstorms rolled in, watching the water swell fast and muddy after hours of heavy rain. When I returned for a visit two years ago, the river had undergone a “beautification project”: the uneven stone steps were replaced with smooth granite paving, the wild reed banks were cleared for a rubberized walking trail, neon signs for river-view milk tea shops and glamping sites glowed along the shore. I leaned down, dipped a finger in the current, and that familiar cool, slightly mossy, faintly fishy scent wrapped around me instantly — and for a split second, I was seven again, my cotton shorts soaked through from wading, my grandma yelling from the porch that I would catch a cold if I didn’t come inside for dinner. That is the quiet magic Chi captures so well: the river does not care about urban renewal projects, about the passage of decades, about how many miles you travel to build a life in a skyscraper-lined city. It holds the version of you that was once small, unburdened, fully rooted in the world, and it keeps that version safe, bobbing gently on the current, for whenever you come back to look for it.

So much of the nostalgia we consume today feels hollow and performative: curated social media reels of “authentic old hometown” snacks, commercialized ancient towns selling identical mass-produced keychains, viral essays mourning a “lost rural China” that feels generic, unrooted, stripped of all the messy, specific, human texture that makes a place feel like home. *The River of My Hometown* pushes gently back against that manufactured longing. Chi never argues that we should all abandon our city lives to move back to our childhood villages and freeze time in the 1980s. She simply reminds us that home is not a zip code, not a stack of faded polaroids, not a list of childhood treats you can now order with two taps on a food delivery app. It is a current that runs through your bones, long after you have learned to navigate the concrete “rivers” of city highways, long after you have forgotten the exact lilt of your grandfather’s laugh, long after you have grown used to falling asleep to the hum of traffic instead of the gurgle of water outside your window.

At the end of the essay, Chi writes that when her time comes, she wants a handful of her ashes scattered in the Emur River, too — not out of grief or a refusal to move on, but because the river was where she first learned what it means to be alive: to feel cold water lapping at bare ankles, to watch something shift and change and keep pushing forward no matter what obstacles block its path, to know that even when you are gone, something you loved deeply will keep flowing, carrying small pieces of everyone who ever cared for it onward, to places you might never get to see.
I closed the book as a long, low-slung cargo barge drifted down Suzhou Creek, its wake rippling the reflections of glass skyscrapers towering above the bank. For a second, if I listened past the honk of car horns and the chatter of passing tourists, I swear I could hear the gurgle of that small river behind my grandma’s house, too — running, always running, holding all of our half-forgotten stories soft and safe in its current.
